title: Unable to open BlueStacks 5 using CmdPal.
author: karedoea
summary: CmdPal discovers the BlueStacks shortcut but Windows returns access denied; the same parameterized shortcut reportedly fails in Flow Launcher, so shortcut properties remain decisive.

status.label: Low-confidence shortcut-launch fix candidate
status.detail: Preserve shell-link arguments and launch semantics only if direct Windows launch proves the shortcut is valid.

next_action.label: Request direct shortcut behavior and properties
next_action.reason: Cross-launcher failure may be caused by the shortcut target, arguments, working directory, or elevation rather than CmdPal.

judgment.rationale: The issue and diagnostic log identify a precise CmdPal launch boundary: AppCommand.StartExe receives the .lnk path and Windows returns access denied. However, the reporter also sees parameterized links fail in Flow Launcher, so a CmdPal-only fix would be speculative until direct shell launch and shortcut properties are known.
evidence: CmdPal discovers and displays the BlueStacks 5 .lnk result.
The diagnostic log records AppCommand.StartExe failing to start the Start Menu .lnk with access denied.
Current CmdPal AppCommand.StartExe uses Process.Start with UseShellExecute=true and passes only the path.
The reporter says links with extra startup parameters fail in both CmdPal and Flow Launcher.
The issue has no linked PR, assignee, or duplicate that resolves the launch path.
Recent AppCommand history concerns command/icon synchronization, not shortcut launch semantics.
judgment.recommended_action: Collect direct double-click behavior and sanitized shortcut properties, then implement only the launch-semantics change supported by those facts.

fix_assessment.rationale: A repository change may be applicable in CmdPal's shortcut launch path, but the shared failure across launchers makes the current plan deliberately low-confidence until Windows itself is shown to launch the shortcut.

proposed_fixes.title: Launch CmdPal shortcuts with their preserved shell-link semantics
proposed_fixes.root_cause: CmdPal launches a discovered .lnk by passing its path to Process.Start, but the shortcut may require shell-link target, arguments, working directory, or elevation semantics that are not preserved by the current path-only launch path.
plan: Inspect src/modules/cmdpal/ext/Microsoft.CmdPal.Ext.Apps/Programs/Win32Program.cs and ShellLinkHelper.cs to confirm whether AppItem.ExePath is the original .lnk or a resolved target and whether arguments/working directory/elevation are retained.

Compare the CmdPal launch path in AppCommand.StartExe with Windows shell behavior for the exact shortcut; choose ShellExecute/verb or ProcessStartInfo fields only after sanitized shortcut properties confirm the required semantics.
Keep packaged-app activation unchanged and scope the change to non-packaged shortcut items.
Add a focused test seam for launch-info construction, covering plain .lnk, arguments, working directory, and administrator verb without starting a process.
Validate against the exact BlueStacks shortcut and a normal shortcut, including direct shell launch as the control.
verification: Open the exact .lnk directly from the Start Menu folder; record whether Windows itself succeeds.
Run CmdPal with the same shortcut and verify BlueStacks launches with its arguments and expected elevation.
Run an ordinary executable and a shortcut without arguments to ensure no regression.
If direct launch also fails, mark the CmdPal hypothesis unsupported and do not apply a competing code fix.

confidence.rationale: CmdPal's path-only Process.Start boundary is concrete, but the same failure in another launcher suggests the shortcut or Windows policy may be the real cause.

issue_context.summary: CmdPal shows the BlueStacks 5 shortcut but pressing Enter produces no launch; logs show access denied.
known_information: The reporter uses PowerToys 0.101.2362.0 on Windows 11 Pro 25H2.
CmdPal discovers the Start Menu .lnk and AppCommand.StartExe logs access denied.
AppCommand.StartExe uses Process.Start with UseShellExecute=true and only the path.
The reporter says parameterized .lnk files also fail in Flow Launcher.
A maintainer discussion identifies HRESULT 0x80070005 in the diagnostic.
inferences: The failure is after discovery, in launch or Windows shell policy.
Missing arguments, working directory, or elevation may matter.
The common failure across launchers makes a shortcut/configuration cause at least as plausible as a CmdPal defect.
issue_context.analysis: The launch boundary is identifiable and supports a testable low-confidence plan, but direct Windows behavior and sanitized properties are required before selecting the correct API or claiming CmdPal ownership.
initial_investigation: Read the complete issue and all six comments, including the diagnostic excerpt and Flow Launcher comparison.
Inspected AppCommand.StartExe, CmdPal Win32Program, and ShellLinkHelper source.
Checked recent AppCommand history and found no shortcut-launch fix.

information_gaps.information: Whether the exact BlueStacks .lnk opens when double-clicked directly.
information_gaps.why_needed: Separates CmdPal behavior from a shortcut or Windows access-control failure.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Double-click the same link from C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs.

information_gaps.information: Sanitized Target, Start in, arguments, and Run as administrator setting.
information_gaps.why_needed: Determines which shell-launch semantics must be preserved.
information_gaps.how_to_collect: Share shortcut Properties values with personal paths and identifiers removed.

design.root_cause: Possible loss of shortcut launch semantics at CmdPal.AppCommand.StartExe, but the cross-launcher failure means the root cause is not established.
evidence: AppCommand.StartExe passes a .lnk path to Process.Start.
The diagnostic records access denied for that path.
Flow Launcher reportedly fails for the same parameterized-link class.

affected_files.purpose: Invokes packaged and non-packaged CmdPal app results.
Creates app items from executables and shortcuts.
Reads target and metadata from Windows shortcuts.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Non-packaged results are launched with Process.Start(path) and UseShellExecute=true.
implementation_steps.change: Construct launch information from the original shortcut metadata only when confirmed necessary, preserving arguments/working directory/verb; otherwise retain the current shell launch.
implementation_steps.code_block: var startInfo = app.IsShortcut ? BuildShortcutStartInfo(app) : new ProcessStartInfo(app.ExePath) { UseShellExecute = true }; Process.Start(startInfo);
edge_cases: Do not bypass Windows elevation prompts.
Do not resolve away required shortcut arguments.
Surface launch errors through the existing logger and preserve dismissal behavior.
tests: Test launch-info construction without starting a process.
Cover plain executable, plain shortcut, parameterized shortcut, and administrator shortcut.

verify: Run the existing CmdPal Apps tests after locating the targeted command.
Compare direct Explorer launch and CmdPal launch for the exact shortcut.
Confirm normal executable and shortcut launch behavior remains unchanged.
risks: Incorrectly reconstructing a shortcut can drop quoting or elevation semantics.
If Windows itself rejects the link, changing CmdPal may not help.
alternatives: Resolve every link to its target and call Process.Start(target): rejected because it can lose arguments and working-directory semantics.
Ignore the issue as external: rejected until direct shell launch is tested.

actions.label: Request direct shortcut behavior and properties

comment.body: Thanks for the diagnostic details. CmdPal finds BlueStacks 5.lnk, then Windows returns access denied; because you also see parameterized links fail in Flow Launcher, we first need to separate a CmdPal launch bug from a shortcut or Windows restriction. Please check whether the exact link opens when double-clicked from C:\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs, and share sanitized shortcut Properties values for Target, Start in, arguments, and Run as administrator.
